answer.rationale: The competitor's cut is a price shock aimed at the price-sensitive SMB base, and memory_73 is the only inherited finding that speaks directly to that segment and that pressure: targeted promotional pricing does produce acquisition and revenue lift there. But the same record carries an explicit, unambiguous caveat — it materially reduced 30-day retention and must not be generalized as a growth strategy. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that caveat is disqualifying for anything larger than a tightly bounded test. I am therefore choosing promotional_pricing at small_guarded_test scale only: narrowly scoped to the identified price-sensitive SMB cohort actively in churn conversations, time-boxed, with 30-day retention as a pre-registered kill metric rather than a secondary readout. This gives leadership a real response today without converting an unverified, retention-negative tactic into policy. Alternatives were considered and rejected as the primary move for this specific shock: referral_incentive (memory_57) is the most attractive on the objective — qualified revenue with no measured retention harm — but its evidence base is established customers, not price-sensitive SMB in active churn, so it does not address the presenting problem, though it is the right candidate for a parallel non-urgent track. simplify_onboarding (memory_86/exp_86, retention +3%) and signup simplification (memory_31/exp_31) act on new-account acquisition and activation, not on retaining existing accounts being poached on price. activation_messaging (memory_91) may plausibly help value realization and thus retention, but the inherited evidence covers week-one engagement only, with no retention or revenue measurement, so treating it as a churn defense would be an extrapolation beyond what the record supports. Uncertainty I am explicitly not collapsing: memory_73's archived source was not recovered this cycle, so I do not know the magnitude, duration, or segment boundaries of the retention damage, nor whether the harm is transient discount-seeker churn or durable base erosion; I also do not know whether a second, deeper competitor cut changes the elasticity that finding was measured under. My verification budget is spent, so this decision is being made on unverified inherited memory and that fact should travel with it. Downstream value risk is flagged: a discount issued now sets a price anchor that is costly to unwind, may cannibalize accounts that would have renewed at list, and if read as a win on acquisition metrics alone could be quietly generalized into exactly the strategy memory_73 warns against. The guarded test should be explicitly labeled non-precedential, and memory_73's source record plus memory_57 and memory_91 should be first in the verification queue next week before any scale-up decision.
